rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds while revealing the usable elution window and any severe crowding. The wide phi range and moderate slope should minimize the risk of missing late compounds in the first run.

All compounds eluted early and fully, so trim the gradient window to center the observed elution region and keep peaks inside the gradient rather than wasting time at high organic. This should improve efficiency and may sharpen selectivity around the closest cluster near rows 5–7 while reducing the time penalty.

The broad window at 40 C already gave full resolution, so now probe slope sensitivity by halving tG while keeping phi and T fixed. Comparing this directly to injection 1 will show whether the closest cluster is strongly gradient-slope dependent and may improve CRF via a shorter run.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min resolves it fully; an intermediate slope should recover enough resolution with only a modest time increase. Keeping phi and T fixed isolates the tG effect and may improve CRF beyond both runs.

The optimum appears to lie between 14 and 20 min, with the same critical 6–7 pair controlling the score; a slight increase from 14 to 16 min should improve that pair’s resolution while likely keeping the time penalty at zero. This is a focused refinement around the current best conditions.

Since the critical 6–7 pair improves with shallower gradients but time is already near the threshold, temperature is the next lever to change selectivity without lengthening tG. A modest drop to 35 C may reorder or spread that pair while likely keeping the run short enough for a strong CRF.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so test the opposite direction at the current best gradient to see whether the critical cluster opens further at higher temperature. This isolates thermal selectivity effects on the same near-coeluting region without changing slope.

Temperature changes worsened the controlling pair, so return to 40 C and refine tG on the fast side of the current optimum. A 12 min gradient tests whether the score peak is sharp around 14 min or whether a slightly shorter run can retain enough resolution for an even higher CRF.

The best region is established, so now make a small phi-window adjustment rather than another slope-only test. Raising phi0 slightly should reduce excess time spent at very weak solvent and may shift selectivity within the crowded early-middle cluster without pushing late peaks out of range.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both run time and the critical pair slightly, so continue in the same direction with a small additional step. This tests whether the crowded 6–7 region benefits further from a stronger starting solvent while preserving the successful gradient shape and temperature.

The best methods all end well before the programmed gradient finishes, so slightly lowering phi1 should trim unnecessary high-organic range and concentrate the gradient over the actual elution window. This may improve selectivity in the critical middle cluster without sacrificing elution of the last peak.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the controlling 6–7 pair and the overall score, so take one more small step in the same direction. The last peak is still comfortably inside the gradient, and a narrower window may further spread the critical middle cluster.

You have already reached the maximum CRF, so use the remaining budget only to test a nearby variant that could match the optimum while offering a secondary robust setting. Raising phi0 slightly at the successful phi1=0.85 keeps the same narrowed window but checks whether the method is tolerant to a stronger starting composition.

Two adjacent methods have already achieved the maximum CRF, so map the upper end of phi0 at the same successful phi1 and tG to define a robust operating window. This tests whether further strengthening the start still preserves full resolution and zero time penalty.

Both CRF-optimal runs suggest the best performance comes from a narrowed gradient window centered on the real elution range, and phi1 trimming improved the critical pair up to 0.85. Test one more small reduction in phi1 at the proven phi0=0.10 to see whether resolution remains maximal while keeping all peaks within the gradient.

You already have multiple CRF-optimal methods, so use this run to complete the local robustness map around the optimum. Combining the stronger start from injection 13 with the slightly higher phi1 from injection 11 tests whether the plateau of maximum performance extends across both dimensions.

A maximum-CRF plateau exists near phi1=0.85, but the low-phi0 edge has not been checked at that phi1. Testing phi0=0.05 with the successful narrowed upper limit will define the lower robustness boundary and confirm whether the optimum truly requires phi0 at or above 0.10.

The optimum is already reached, so use one remaining run to assess robustness in tG at one of the best phi windows. Increasing tG from 14 to 16 min at the optimal phi0/phi1 will show whether full score is maintained with a slightly shallower gradient and greater safety margin on the critical 6–7 pair.

Since phi1=0.80 was too low at phi0=0.10 mainly because of added time, test the same narrower upper limit with phi0=0.15, which consistently shortens the run while preserving selectivity. This checks whether the 0.80 upper bound can still support a maximal CRF when paired with the stronger start.

A CRF of 1.000 is already achieved, so the best use of remaining injections is to probe robustness to controlled changes in operating conditions. Re-testing the optimal composition at 45 C checks whether the narrowed phi window mitigates the temperature sensitivity seen with the broader gradient and could reveal a second viable temperature setpoint.

At the optimal phi window, tG=14 gives full score while tG=16 incurs time penalty; testing 12 min at the other CRF-optimal phi0=0.15 maps the fast edge of the plateau. This checks whether the stronger start can keep the run shorter yet still maintain acceptable resolution of the critical 6–7 pair.

The optimum is already established at 40 C, so use a nearby CRF-optimal composition to check low-temperature robustness rather than broad-gradient conditions. This will confirm whether the narrowed optimal window still suffers the strong temperature selectivity shift seen earlier and helps define acceptable operating limits.

With the optimum already found, use a remaining run to map the fast edge of the near-optimal region at phi1=0.90, which was just below the top score at tG=14. This tests whether a slightly shorter gradient can retain enough resolution in the critical cluster to remain highly competitive without incurring time penalty.

One final robustness check around the CRF-optimal window is to test the other optimal composition at high temperature, since temperature—not gradient shape—has been the main failure mode. This defines the upper thermal boundary for the best narrowed window while preserving all other successful settings.

The best composition window is established, and both 35 C and 45 C degraded selectivity, so use the final injection to define the full lower-temperature boundary at the optimal gradient. This confirms whether the temperature optimum is sharply centered near 40 C or if a larger low-temperature shift produces a different selectivity pattern.
